Example Code
from fastapi import FastAPI
import logging
import uvicorn
import sys

FMT = "%(asctime)s %(levelname)s [%(name)s] trace_id=%(otelTraceID)s span_id=%(otelSpanID)s resource.service.name=%(otelServiceName)s | %(message)s"

console = logging.StreamHandler(stream=sys.stdout)
console.setFormatter(logging.Formatter(FMT))

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
logger.addHandler(console)
logger.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)


app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/")
def index():
    logger.info("Handling request")
    return {"hello": "world"}


@app.middleware("http")
async def middle(request, call_next):
    logger.info("In middleware, before call_next()")
    response = await call_next(request)
    logger.info("In middleware, after call_next()")
    return response


if __name__ == '__main__':
    log_config = uvicorn.config.LOGGING_CONFIG
    log_config["formatters"]["access"]["fmt"] = FMT
    logger.info("Starting app...")
    uvicorn.run("__main__:app", host='0.0.0.0', port=8082, log_config=log_config, reload=False)
Description
In a Python/Uvicorn/FastAPI application, auto-instrumented with OpenTelemetry through opentelemetry-bootstrap -a install and opentelemetry-instrument python main.py, the use of a HTTP middleware seems to lose the request context that allows OpenTelemetry to know about the current span and its spanId/traceId.
Note: I'm not sure if I should be asking/reporting this here, or in Starlette, or Uvicorn, or OpenTelemetry 😬

As during local development your app directory is mounted as a volume inside the container, you can also run the migrations with alembic commands inside the container and the migration code will be in your app directory (instead of being only inside the container). So you can add it to your git repository.
Make sure you create a "revision" of your models and that you "upgrade" your database with that revision every time you change them. As this is what will update the tables in your database. Otherwise, your application will have errors.

Commit to Help

 I commit to help with one of those options 👆

Example Code
I have this annoying situation where I have to handle a lot of exceptions with the same handler. An extra *args coud be added in the exception_handler method in order to be able to do something like this:


@app.exception_handler(UserNotFound, AccountNotFound, EmailNotFound, SessionNotFound)
async def handle_not_found(request, exc):
    return HTTPException(
        status_code=status.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND,
        detail=str(exc)
    )

@app.exception_handler(EmailAlreadyExists, UserAlreadyExists)
async def email_already_exists(request, exc):
    return HTTPException(
        status_code=status.HTTP_409_CONFLICT,
        detail=str(exc)
    )

Instead of writting a handler for every single exception type or status code. It doesn't break backward compatiblity.
Description
In the exception handler:
    def exception_handler(
        self,
        exc_class_or_status_code: Annotated[
            Union[int, Type[Exception]],
            Doc(
                """
                The Exception class this would handle, or a status code.
                """
            ),
        ],
        *extra_exc_classes_or_status_codes: Annotated[
            Union[int, Type[Exception]],
            Doc(
                """
                Extra Exception classs this would handle, or a status codes.
                """
            ),
        ],
    ) -> Callable[[DecoratedCallable], DecoratedCallable]:
Extra attributes could be added. And they can be be implemented simply like this:
    def decorator(func: DecoratedCallable) -> DecoratedCallable:
        self.add_exception_handler(exc_class_or_status_code, func)
        for extra_exc_class_or_status_code in extra_exc_classes_or_status_codes:
            self.add_exception_handler(extra_exc_class_or_status_code , func)
        return func
An that's it. Doesn't break barckard compatibility, or add any complexity.

nodes.body:
First Check

 I added a very descriptive title here.

Commit to Help

 I commit to help with one of those options 👆

Example Code
# This is the code from the existing docs:
# https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/body-fields/

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    description: str | None = Field(
        default=None, title="The description of the item", max_length=300
    )
    price: float = Field(gt=0, description="The price must be greater than zero")
    tax: float | None = None
Description
There appear to be two ways to define Fields (like Query) in FastAPI: using the annotated method or the default value:
https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/fields/#the-annotated-pattern
https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/query-params-str-validations/
# Option 1
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class Model(BaseModel):
    int_list: list[Annotated[int, Field(gt=0)]]


# Option 2
class Model(BaseModel):
    int_list: list[int] = Field(gt=0)
In the query docs, it is recommended to use Option 1, the Annotated type, for various reasons. However, the Field docs don't mention this advantage at all, and both the default example and the "non-Annotated" variant use the same pattern of Option 2.
Is it preferable to use Annotated for Body Fields, just like it is recommended for Query parameters?
If so - should we update the Body Field documentation to reflect that?
If not - should we at least document both variations in the Body Field docs?

nodes.author: alv2017
nodes.body:
Is it preferable to use Annotated for Body Fields, just like it is recommended for Query parameters?

No, Pydantic supports the use Annotated Fields, but it doesn't claim that it is a recommended approach. (There are pros and cons, and developers are free to choose what works best for them)

If so - should we update the Body Field documentation to reflect that?

I don't think so

If not - should we at least document both variations in the Body Field docs?

I don't think so, this is rather about how to use Pydantic (and not the FastAPI). The best way to learn about Pydantic features is to consult the Pydantic documentation.
(imho)

nodes.author: YuriiMotov
nodes.body:
It depends on whether you interact with server how it expects or not.
from fastapi import FastAPI, WebSocketDisconnect
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from fastapi.websockets import WebSocket
import pytest

app = FastAPI()

@app.websocket("/ws")
async def websocket(websocket: WebSocket):
    # Send data and close connection
    await websocket.accept()
    await websocket.send_json({"msg": "Hello WebSocket"})
    await websocket.close()

# ====  Tests  ====

def test_websocket():
    # Connect to server, receive data from server, server closes connection
    client = TestClient(app)
    with client.websocket_connect("/ws") as websocket:
        data = websocket.receive_json()
        assert data == {"msg": "Hello WebSocket"}

In the code example above everything is as server expects: client connected, server sends data to client and closes connection (exit endpoint function).
In the next code example, server expects data from user.
from fastapi import FastAPI, WebSocketDisconnect
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from fastapi.websockets import WebSocket
import pytest

app = FastAPI()

@app.websocket("/ws2")
async def websocket2(websocket: WebSocket):
    # Wait for data from the client and then close connection
    await websocket.accept()
    await websocket.receive_json()  # Wait for data from client
    await websocket.close()

# ====  Tests  ====

def test_websocket2():
    # Connect to server, send data to server, server recieves data and closes connection
    client = TestClient(app)
    with client.websocket_connect("/ws2") as websocket:
        websocket.send_json({"msg": "Hello WebSocket"})


def test_websocket2_clientside_close():
    # Connect to server, server is waiting for data, but we just close connection
    client = TestClient(app)
    with pytest.raises(WebSocketDisconnect):
        with client.websocket_connect("/ws2") as _websocket:
            pass  # Do not send data, just close connection

If we do send data (test_websocket2), server receives data and closes connection.
But if we don't send data and just close connection (test_websocket2_clientside_close), WebSocketDisconnect exception is raised inside the endpoint.
Usually we handle this exception inside the endpoint function:
from fastapi import FastAPI, WebSocketDisconnect
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from fastapi.websockets import WebSocket

app = FastAPI()


@app.websocket("/ws2")
async def websocket2(websocket: WebSocket):
    # Wait for data from the client and then close connection
    await websocket.accept()
    try:
        await websocket.receive_json()
        await websocket.close()
    except WebSocketDisconnect:
        pass

# ====  Tests  ====

def test_websocket2_clientside_close():
    # Connect to server, server is waiting for data, but we just close connection
    client = TestClient(app, raise_server_exceptions=False)
    with client.websocket_connect("/ws2") as _websocket:
        pass  # Do not send data, just close connection

nodes.body:
So, as I understand, this is what you needed:
from collections.abc import Awaitable, Callable
from typing import Annotated, Optional

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, HTTPException, Request
from fastapi.security import HTTPBearer

class ValidateHTTPBearer(HTTPBearer):
    def __init__(
        self,
        *,
        scheme_name: Optional[str] = None,
        other_validations: list[Callable[[str], Awaitable[None]]],
    ):
        super().__init__(scheme_name=scheme_name)
        self._other_validations = other_validations

    async def validate_parse_token(self, token: str) -> dict:
        data = token.split(":")
        return {"user": data[0], "something": data[1]}

    async def validate_current_user(self, parsed_token: dict) -> str:
        return parsed_token["user"]

    async def __call__(self, request: Request) -> str:
        # Call the parent class to get the credentials
        auth_credentials = await super().__call__(request)

        # Validate the token and user
        parsed_token = await self.validate_parse_token(auth_credentials.credentials)
        user = await self.validate_current_user(parsed_token)

        # Perform other validations
        token_data = parsed_token.copy()
        token_data["user"] = user
        for validation in self._other_validations:
            await validation(token_data)

        return user


async def validate_token(token_data: dict):
    if token_data["something"] != "123":
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Invalid token")

async def validate_user(token_data: dict):
    if token_data.get("user") != "admin":
        raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="Invalid user")

security = ValidateHTTPBearer(
    scheme_name="SomeBearer",
    other_validations=[validate_token, validate_user]
)

CurrentUser = Annotated[str, Depends(security)]

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/")
def index(current_user: CurrentUser):
    return {"user": current_user}
And the answer to your question:

Now I want to understand how is Async call being invoked and from where it is awaited?

FastAPI analyzes dependencies of the endpoint and calls\awaits them depending on the function signature.
Once you pass the instance of ValidateHTTPBearer as a dependency, it looks at the signature of __call__ method and awaits it

Can't reproduce the error you mentioned.
But in general, don't use the results of dependencies with yield in StreamingResponse generators. Session created this way will be closed right after returning from the endpoint function.
async def get_async_db():
    try:
        async with async_session() as db:
            print("db session created")
            yield db
    finally:
        print("db session closed")

# generator for StreamingResponse
async def mock_generator(db: AsyncSession):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    print("attempting to use db session")
    user = await db.scalar(select(User).filter(User.id == 1)) # replace it with your own database query
    yield user.name


@app.get("/", response_class=StreamingResponse)
async def end_pint(
    db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_async_db),
):
    return StreamingResponse(content=mock_generator(db=db))
Output (attempt to use closed session):
INFO:     Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:8000 (Press CTRL+C to quit)
db session created
db session closed
INFO:     127.0.0.1:58070 - "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 OK
attempting to use db session

Instead, pass session maker to it and open session inside:
import uvicorn
import asyncio
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import async_sessionmaker
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine
from sqlalchemy import Column, Integer, String, select
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi import Depends
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase

class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass

class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "user"
    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True, index=True)
    name = Column(String(50), index=True)

# database connection
async_engine = create_async_engine(
    "sqlite+aiosqlite://"
)

Example Code
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request

app = FastAPI()
import asyncio

def reloaded_stream(request_body: RequestModel, server_request: Request) -> StreamingResponse:
    async def stream_from_disconnected_llm() -> AsyncGenerator[bytes, None]:
        yielded_all_chunks = False
        while not yielded_all_chunks:
            try:
                chunk = await asyncio.wait_for(app.state.llm_response[request_body.request_id]["queue"].get(), timeout=5)
                async with app.state.lock:
                    finished = app.state.llm_response[request_body.request_id]["finished"]
                    if finished and app.state.llm_response[request_body.request_id]["queue"].qsize() == 0:
                        yielded_all_chunks = True
                app.state.llm_response[request_body.request_id]["queue"].task_done()
                yield chunk
            except asyncio.TimeoutError:
                pass 
        

    return StreamingResponse(
        stream_from_disconnected_llm(),
        media_type="text/event-stream",
        headers={"Cache-Control": "no-cache", "Connection": "keep-alive", "Transfer-Encoding": "chunked"},
    )


def streaming_response(request_body: RequestModel, server_request: Request) -> StreamingResponse:
    async def stream_with_cancel() -> AsyncGenerator[bytes, None]:
        try:
            #Dummy func that streams LLM response
            stream_coroutine = generate_chat_message_stream()
            async for chunk in stream_coroutine:
                if await server_request.is_disconnected():
                    #What I want to happen, but instead goes to the CancelledError exception
                    await app.state.llm_response[request_body.request_id]["queue"].put(chunk.encode('utf-8'))
                else:
                    yield chunk.encode('utf-8')
            async with app.state.lock:
                app.state.llm_response[request_body.request_id]["finished"] = True
            print("Returning")
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            print("Disconnected streaming responses always go here")
            raise
    return StreamingResponse(
        stream_with_cancel(),
        media_type="text/event-stream",
        headers={"Cache-Control": "no-cache", "Connection": "keep-alive", "Transfer-Encoding": "chunked"},
    )


@app.post("/")
async def generate(request: RequestModel, server_request: Request):
    if not hasattr(app.state, "llm_response"):
        app.state.llm_response = {}
        app.state.lock = asyncio.Lock()
        app.state.request_set = set()
    if request.request_id in app.state.request_set:
        return reloaded_stream(request, server_request)
    else:
        app.state.request_set.add(request.request_id)
        app.state.llm_response[request.request_id] = {"queue": asyncio.Queue(), "finished": False}
        return streaming_response(request, server_request)

I want the functionality, that if someone sends a request to an LLM, and then they reload the page during the response, the information will still be sent. Currently how I aim to do that is by detecting a client disconnect through Request.is_disconnected(), and then putting the chunks in a queue in the state attribute of FastAPI, and then streaming from the queue with a second request that is given the same request id. But from my testing, and from what these two links talk about: #7572 and this blog, it seems like a StreamingResponse will automatically detect for a client disconnect and raise a asyncio.CancelledError exception. Is there any way to stop this from occurring, either through how the StreamingResponse is called or otherwise?

nodes.author: YuriiMotov
nodes.body:
StreamingResponse will automatically detect for a client disconnect and raise a asyncio.CancelledError exception. Is there any way to stop this from occurring

No, there is no such option.
I think the only way to achieve what you want is to run async task (using asyncio.create_task) that will generate data and save it somewhere. And, the generator function of StreamingResponse should take that saved data and return it.
Then, if client send request with the same id, you can take that saved data and return it instead of generating it again.
import asyncio
import dataclasses
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse


@dataclasses.dataclass
class GeneratedData:
    last_sent: int = -1
    finished: bool = False
    chunks: list[bytes] = dataclasses.field(default_factory=list)


data_storage: dict[str, GeneratedData] = {}


async def data_generator(generated_data: GeneratedData):
    for i in range(5):
        await asyncio.sleep(1)
        print("Generating data chunk", i)
        generated_data.chunks.append(f"Chunk {i}".encode())
    generated_data.finished = True


async def send_data_generator(generated_data: GeneratedData):
    i = generated_data.last_sent + 1
    while (i < len(generated_data.chunks)) or (not generated_data.finished):
        if i < len(generated_data.chunks):
            print("Send data chunk", i)
            yield generated_data.chunks[i]
            generated_data.last_sent = i
            i += 1
        else:
            await asyncio.sleep(0.1)


app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/", response_class=StreamingResponse)
async def end_pint(
    req_id: str,
):
    if req_id not in data_storage:
        data_storage[req_id] = GeneratedData()
        asyncio.create_task(data_generator(data_storage[req_id]))

    return StreamingResponse(send_data_generator(generated_data=data_storage[req_id]))

nodes.author: luzzodev
nodes.body:
Hello @y2kbugger i'll try to explain what is wrong in your code and what is happening.
The problem with your code is that the deadlock happens due to thread exhaustion.
Basically the depency c: Annotated[GlobalCounter, Depends(get_counter) is the one that is exhausting the threadpool due the lock and since your endpoint function is sync ( so need a thread ), at some point you will not have any available thread to execute it and since you cannot execute it your dependency will never be released and with that the lock.
A short simple example: suppose to limit the pool to 2 threads and the are 3 incoming requests.
r1 -> solve dependency and lock
r2 -> trying solve dependecy and is wait for the lock
r3 -> is waiting for a thread
r1 with the dependecy solved, now try to call the endpoint function but is sync so need a thread where can be executed but there are no thread available. Here all is blocked forever.
In your second example where you have all inside the endpoint all works because only the endpoint thread is required and you are already inside it.
To fix the first example, just trasform
def increment_dep(c: Annotated[GlobalCounter, Depends(get_counter)]) -> None:
in
async def increment_dep(c: Annotated[GlobalCounter, Depends(get_counter)]) -> None:
In general i would suggest to avoid locks inside the dependency, because you are basically serializing the requests and bringing complexity with it.

FastAPI automatically returns a 404 Not Found response when accessing an unknown route. However, this does not raise an exception, meaning observability tools like Honeycomb do not capture it as an error.

Create a simple FastAPI app

nodes.author: luzzodev
nodes.body:
Hello @wu-clan, @JavierSanchezCastro, the problem is not fastapi-cli neither in uvicorn.
This has to deal with how uvicorn import modules, when you pass a string as argument. Under the hood the importlib.import_module is used and in your example this is what is happening.
# main.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
import uvicorn

app = FastAPI()

print("Hello!")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    uvicorn.run("main:app", host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)
The first time you load the main.py the module name is not main but  __main__, so in the import cache will be set the module __name__.
At this point your execution will arrive at
uvicorn.run("main:app", host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)
Uvicorn will use importlib.import_module
importlib.import_module("main") -> but main is not the import cache so will loaded and thats why you see double print.
You can test using this code
from fastapi import FastAPI
import uvicorn

app = FastAPI()

print("Hello!", __name__)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    uvicorn.run("uvi_rerun:app", host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)
At this point you can fix your code structure and your code, knowing what is happening.

nodes.body:
This has an open PR here: #13464

First Check

Commit to Help

 I commit to help with one of those options 👆

Example Code
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from fastapi import FastAPI, Form

class MyModel(BaseModel):
    checkbox: bool = True

app = FastAPI()

@app.post("/")
def form_endpoint(model: Annotated[MyModel, Form()]):
    # doesn't matter what happens here, bug is during model instantiation
    pass
Description
This is distinct from these prior issues -

#11852
#9409
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/73078330/fastapi-request-body-returns-null-from-checkbox-html-tag

HTML forms submit no value when a checkbox is unchecked, and submit a string (default "on" when checked). By the time the value is received by the pydantic model, either through a field or a model validator, it either is a) the explicitly provided string value, or b) the default value.
If the default value is True, it is impossible to differentiate an explicit True from a default True in the model itself, so one can't write a model validator that can be used both with the form input case and programmatic usage.
Since the problem is a matter of the HTML standards not providing a bool, checkboxes are unambiguously booleans, the boolean status is invisible at the point of model instantiation but NOT at the point that FastAPI parses the form data (not present is False and a string is True), it should be the FastAPI form handling logic that casts it to a bool prior to reaching the model. This would resolve the above issues as well without needing to resort to awkward workarounds.
The prior workarounds do not apply to this case, since there either were no defaults or the defaults were False - the problem in this case is specifically that a default of True is not possible with form inputs.
I am more than happy to write a PR for this if maintainers agree :)
This is the only way i have found to make it work, but it is very not DRY to have to do this for every checkbox in a way that is not bundled with the model.
@app.post("/form")
async def endpoint(
    request: Request,
    model: Annotated[MyModel, Form()],
):
    form = await request.form()
    model.checkbox = "checkbox" in form

nodes.title: ContextVars in sync vs async dependencies

nodes.author: jgould22
nodes.body:
The TL;DR appears to be that FastAPI treats synchronous dependencies in a separate thread to the one handling the request, thereby causing issues with the way ContextVar handles values internally. The same issue is not present with asynchronous dependencies.

This is not a bug, and is expected behaviour. FastAPI makes the assumption that a sync dependency has blocking code in it (otherwise why not use async) since FastAPI is an async first framework it spawns these dependencies onto a thread pool so as not to block the event loop. This will have implications for context vars.

nodes.title: Thread-Based CPU-Bound Tasks Cause High Latency
nodes.body:
First Check

 I added a very descriptive title here.
 I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it.
 I searched the FastAPI documentation, with the integrated search.
 I already searched in Google "How to X in FastAPI" and didn't find any information.
 I already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer.
 I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to Pydantic.
 I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to Swagger UI.
 I already checked if it is not related to FastAPI but to ReDoc.

Commit to Help

 I commit to help with one of those options 👆

Example Code
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

from fastapi import FastAPI, Response

app = FastAPI()

# Global process pool for offloading CPU-bound tasks.
process_pool = ProcessPoolExecutor()


def cpu_bound_task():
    total = 0
    for i in range(10**10):  # Adjust this number for desired running time
        total += i * i
    return total


@app.get("/block-cpu")
def block_cpu():
    """
    Synchronous endpoint that performs a heavy CPU-bound task inline.
    """
    cpu_bound_task()
    return {"message": "Finished CPU task inline"}


@app.get("/block-cpu-process")
def block_cpu_process():
    """
    Endpoint that offloads the CPU-bound task to a separate process.
    """
    future = process_pool.submit(cpu_bound_task)
    future.result()  # Wait for the offloaded task to complete.
    return {"message": "Finished CPU task in process"}


@app.get("/time")
def time_check():
    """
    A simple endpoint that immediately returns a 200 status code.
    """
    return Response(status_code=200)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import uvicorn

    # Start the server using uvicorn.run.
    uvicorn.run("app:app", host="127.0.0.1", port=8000)
Description
Description
I'm experiencing a significant increase in latency on a very simple endpoint when executing a heavy CPU-bound task inline (using the default thread-based workers). In contrast, offloading the same CPU-bound work to a separate process (using a global process pool) keeps the lightweight endpoint responsive.
I expected that, since Python’s Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) is supposed to switch threads approximately every 5ms, the inline CPU-bound task wouldn't block the server for an extended period. However, the observed behavior is that the inline task causes a massive latency increase for other endpoints.

measure_time.sh
This Bash script makes 1000 requests to the /time endpoint, converts the response times to milliseconds, and then calculates and prints the average and standard deviation.
#!/bin/bash
echo "Performing 1000 requests to /time endpoint..."

# Perform 1000 requests, converting each request's time from seconds to milliseconds.
for i in {1..1000}; do
    curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{time_total}\n" http://127.0.0.1:8000/time
done | awk 'BEGIN { min=999999; max=0 }
{
    # Convert seconds to milliseconds.
    t = $1 * 1000;
    sum += t;
    sumsq += (t * t);
    if (t < min) min = t;
    if (t > max) max = t;
    count++;
} END {
    avg = sum / count;
    stddev = sqrt(sumsq / count - avg * avg);
    printf "Performed %d requests\n", count;
    printf "Average: %.4f ms\n", avg;
    printf "Stddev: %.4f ms\n", stddev;
    printf "Min: %.4f ms\n", min;
    printf "Max: %.4f ms\n", max;
}'
Make sure to make the script executable:
chmod +x measure_time.sh

Steps to Reproduce


Start the Server
Run the FastAPI app:
python app.py


Measure Baseline Latency
In a separate terminal, run the measurement script to capture baseline latency of the /time endpoint:
./measure_time.sh


Performing 1000 requests to /time endpoint...
Performed 1000 requests
Average: 0.7302 ms
Stddev: 0.7759 ms




Simulate Heavy CPU Load with Inline Task
In another terminal, launch several concurrent requests to the inline CPU-bound endpoint:
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/block-cpu &
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/block-cpu &
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/block-cpu &
Then, re-run the measurement script:
./measure_time.sh


    Performing 1000 requests to /time endpoint...
    Performed 1000 requests
    Average: 83.4512 ms
    Stddev: 59.2917 ms

Expected Result: The /time endpoint shows dramatically increased latency.


Simulate Heavy CPU Load with Process-Offloaded Task
Restart the existing Python process (to kill the running tasks)
In another terminal, launch several concurrent requests to the process-offloaded endpoint:
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/block-cpu-process &
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/block-cpu-process &
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/block-cpu-process &
Then, re-run the measurement script:
./measure_time.sh
Performing 1000 requests to /time endpoint...
Performed 1000 requests
Average: 9.0379 ms
Stddev: 3.7918 ms

Expected Result: The /time endpoint remains responsive with low latency.



Observed Behavior


Inline CPU-bound Task (/block-cpu):
When the heavy CPU-bound task is executed inline using the thread workers, the latency for the /time endpoint increases dramatically (100x).


Process-Offloaded Task (/block-cpu-process):
Offloading the CPU-bound task to a separate process maintains low latency on the /time endpoint (10x).



Question
Given that the GIL should allow thread switching approximately every 5ms, why does executing a heavy CPU-bound task inline (using threads) cause such a significant latency increase for lightweight endpoints like /time? What factors might be contributing to this behavior, and are there any workarounds within FastAPI or Uvicorn to mitigate the issue without resorting to process-based offloading?

Additional Context
I have searched the FastAPI documentation, Google, and GitHub issues but haven't found an explanation for this behavior. I suspect that the high latency may be due to how the CPU-bound tasks interact with the thread pool and the GIL, but I'm not entirely sure why the expected thread switching does not mitigate the impact.
Thank you for your assistance and any insights you can provide!

Linux

nodes.author: luzzodev
nodes.body:
Hello @alexwilson1,
is always recommended, not only in Fastapi but in python, to run heavy cpu tasks in a different process and not threads.
While is True that the GIL will try to switch thread every few ms, it should have the opportunity to do that.
For example yielding a value, I/O operations and so on.
In your case your just looping and sum a value and that will probably hold the GIL for mutch more time.

nodes.body:
Hi, I'm not sure if you're still facing this issue or not but just wanted to follow up on this. Sorry for the long delay. From this blog:

time_starttransfer is just before cURL reads the first byte from the network (it hasn't actually read it yet). This includes the round trip over the network, .....

So your backend server is taking close to 0.47s to calculate the response before sending it back completely over the network. I'm not sure how much further you can speed this up without vertically scaling your compute but that's all I can help you with for now without taking a good look at the code. Perhaps there are other ways you can speed up your response calculation time but that's beyond the scope of FastAPI's support.

nodes.author: p-hebert
nodes.body:
Found the source of the issue! It was simply a typo in the env var in the tests 🤦‍♂️
This being said, I followed your advice and migrated to the lifespan approach:
app/main.py
# app/main.py

from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from fastapi import FastAPI
from app.lifespan import some_lifespan_ctx

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    async with some_lifespan_ctx():
        yield

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)
app/lifespan.py
import asyncio
import os
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

counter = [0]  # use list because int is immutable and imported by value, not ref

@asynccontextmanager
async def some_lifespan_ctx():
    task = None
    if os.getenv("ACTIVATE_SOME_LIFESPAN_CTX") in ("true", "1"):
        async def poll():
            while True:
                global counter
                counter[0] += 1
                await asyncio.sleep(60)
        task = asyncio.create_task(poll())

    try:
        yield
    finally:
        if task is not None:
            task.cancel()
            try:
                await task
            except asyncio.CancelledError:
                pass
tests/test_lifespan.py
import asyncio
import pytest
from app.lifespan import counter, some_lifespan_ctx

# Use pytest-asyncio for async tests.

@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_lifespan_ctx_no_poll(monkeypatch):
    """
    should not start a polling task when ACTIVATE_SOME_LIFESPAN_CTX is not set to true or 1.
    """
    # arrange: set polling env var to "0" so no polling task is started.
    monkeypatch.setenv("ACTIVATE_SOME_LIFESPAN_CTX", "0")

    async def fake_sleep(duration):
        raise asyncio.CancelledError()  # kill the loop after one iteration

    monkeypatch.setattr(asyncio, "sleep", fake_sleep)

    # act: run the context manager.
    async with some_lifespan_ctx():
        pass

    # assert: since env var is not in (true, 1), the poll loop shouldn't have run.
    assert counter[0] == 0


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_jwks_poller_ctx_with_poll(monkeypatch):
    """
    should start a polling task when ACTIVATE_SOME_LIFESPAN_CTX is set to true or 1.
    """
    # arrange: set polling env var to "1" so polling task is started.
    monkeypatch.setenv("ACTIVATE_SOME_LIFESPAN_CTX", "1")

    async def fake_sleep(duration):
        raise asyncio.CancelledError()  # kill the loop after one iteration

    monkeypatch.setattr(asyncio, "sleep", fake_sleep)

    # act: run the context manager.
    async with some_lifespan_ctx():
        pass

    # assert: since we raise in sleep, counter should be 1
    assert counter[0] == 1
and the tests pass! I haven't tested this simplified version per say, but the real use case has been tested and works :))
Thanks a lot for your help! I'll mark my answer as the resolution, but your help was instrumental! :)

@pytest.mark.asyncio

nodes.body:
In the meantime, while waiting for better solutions: 😄
Please note regarding the @app.middleware decorator:
    """
    We no longer document this decorator style API, and its usage is discouraged.
    Instead you should use the following approach:

    >>> middleware = [Middleware(...), ...]
    >>> app = Starlette(middleware=middleware)
    """

The recommended approach is to use class-based middleware. This is example from Starlette:
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.middleware import Middleware
from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware


class CustomHeaderMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
    async def dispatch(self, request, call_next):
        response = await call_next(request)
        response.headers['Custom'] = 'Example'
        return response

routes = ...

middleware = [
    Middleware(CustomHeaderMiddleware)
]

app = Starlette(routes=routes, middleware=middleware)
The middleware used in FastAPI is coming from Starlette, and Starlette has much more extensive documentation on middlewares: https://www.starlette.io/middleware
For low level operations, like manipulating ASGI scopes, refer the documentation of the application server (uvicorn, or whatever you are using).

import logging

def register_log_filter() -> None:
    """
    Removes logs from healthiness/readiness endpoints so they don't spam
    and pollute application log flow

nodes.author: marsboy02
nodes.body:
q represents an optional query parameter. For example, in the case of reference you send.  if a client makes a request like:
/send-notification/{email}?q=some_query
then q is present. In this case, according to the reference you provided, here's what happens:

A background task is scheduled to write the "message to email" line into log.txt.
Then, another background task is scheduled to write the line "found query: some_query" into log.txt.
Because log.txt is opened in append mode, once the API response is returned, the background tasks run sequentially and both messages are appended to the log.

As mentioned, q is an optional query parameter. Consider the following example:
/send-notification/{email}
In this case, if no query parameter is provided, get_query doesn’t add any extra task, so only "message to email" is logged.
Now, let’s apply similar logic to a /file endpoint with a request like /file?q=some_path. The following logic would occur:

A backup copy of the file is created (with a .bak extension).
A background task is scheduled to delete the backup copy.
Since an optional query parameter is provided (q=some_path), another background task is scheduled to delete some_path.
After the API returns its response, the remaining tasks in the background queue execute.

This behavior might seem odd—it suggests that the optional query parameter might not be necessary. Without knowing all the details of the request and response requirements, it’s hard to say definitively, but I hope this explanation helps. Have a great day!

Hello @gurobokum,

What is the reason to have HTTPBase and derived classes call method async?

Fastapi is an asynchronous framework, all subclasses of HTTPBase  can be used as dependency and for this reason they are async. Each not async dependency is executed in a separated thread to avoid blocking the main loop, so make it sync, would be only inefficient.
About your case: since logfire for fastapi is based on OpenTelemetry FastAPI Instrumentation would be better to attach the user info to the request or a span and read them from there instead of reprocessing the header twice.

nodes.author: luzzodev
nodes.body:
Hello @TanelS,
there is not an official and supported way to do it.
Keeping that in mind, consider the following as a "workaround".
General considerations:
Far small changes that do not impact on route definition, validation. etc. you can modify directly the app.openapi_schema definition. For example if your want to change the title, version, some decription and so on. This operation will not require any reload.
Changes to route definitions, validation, etc., are more complex to handle because modifying the OpenAPI specs alone is not enough to affect FastAPI's request handling flow — unless you have a truly dynamic validation process in place.
Workaround
The app.openapi_schema is not the only thing FastAPI caches — it also caches the routes along with their dependencies. So even if you update your route information and regenerate the API schema, it will still use the 'cached' version of your routes to generate the schema.
What can you do?
- Add the same endpoint again with its updated definition.
- Invalidate the OpenAPI schema by setting app.openapi_schema = None.
- Regenerate the OpenAPI schema (it will now reflect the latest routes).
- Remove the old version of the endpoint.

Why does this work?
- Each route is appended to the router’s internal route list.
- For every incoming request, FastAPI iterates through this list from top to bottom and executes the first matching route.
- OpenAPI schema generation follows the same order — but when duplicate paths exist, the last one overrides the previous definition in the schema.
- Therefore, to fully replace a route, you must remove the earlier version (i.e. the first occurrence of that path/method combo).
  At that point, your newly added endpoint becomes both the active one for requests and the one reflected in the docs.

Note:
All of these changes must be made on the main FastAPI app. Any modifications applied directly to an APIRouter after it has been included in the app will have no effect.
This is an unofficial workaround, so it may break or behave differently in future FastAPI versions — don’t rely on it being officially supported.
Whenever possible, prefer using real dynamic types and properly updating the OpenAPI specs through officially supported means. Only consider hot-reloading or runtime patching when restarting the app is truly not an option.
Hope this helps.

Hello,
I'm working on a project using fastapi and running into an issue with the intermingling of non-async fastapi routes, and async code.
In particular:

My project uses non-async fastapi routes / endpoints (I cannot immediately migrate to async ones)
As part of handling some API requests, I need to use a client library which under the hood makes use of asyncio e.g. via get_event_loop().run_until_complete(some_func)

    get_event_loop().run_until_complete(some_coroutine)
    ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^
  File "/Users/myuser/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.13.2-macos-aarch64-none/lib/python3.13/asyncio/events.py", line 716, in get_event_loop
    raise RuntimeError('There is no current event loop in thread %r.'
                       % threading.current_thread().name)
RuntimeError: There is no current event loop in thread 'AnyIO worker thread'.

My question is twofold:

What is the best way to ensure there is an active event loop without changing every single route? In particular I tried to add a ensure_event_loop_initialized method which makes sure an event loop is indeed initialized at the middleware layer, but it doesnt solve the issue, apparently because the middle ware may run on a different thread than the actual endpoint handler. Similarly, I am able to run it via a depends clause on individual routers , e.g router = APIRouter(dependencies=[Depends(ensure_event_loop_started)]). This seems to work but I read somewhere on the github issues that this is also not guaranteed to be run in same thread as request handling?
How bad is it to have an event loop as part of sync. fastapi request handling functions to begin with? I assume its not ideal but for cases like this where I need to make legacy code work with fastapi is this more or less supported use case?

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.encoders import jsonable_encoder
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
from fastapi.security import APIKeyHeader
from starlette.exceptions import HTTPException

def http_exception_handler(request: Request, exc: HTTPException) -> JSONResponse:
    return JSONResponse(
        jsonable_encoder({
            "success": False,
        }),
        status_code=exc.status_code,
    )

app = FastAPI(
    exception_handlers={
        HTTPException: http_exception_handler,
    },
    dependencies=[Depends(APIKeyHeader(name="keykey"))]
)

@app.get("/")
def root() -> dict[str, str]:
    return {"ping": "pong"}
Description
This codes runs as expected, with the exception handler being executed when you, for example, don't pass the Header.
However, my type checker (VSCode's default one, Pylance/Pyright, I think) gives me a type mismatch on the exception_handlers argument of FastAPI. Indeed, the argument is typed as an optional dict with the value type being Callable[[Request, Any], Coroutine[Any, Any, Response]], which is incompatible with my handler. But should it?
As far as I know, that would be the annotation for an async handler, and indeed declaring my handler as async removes the mismatch. But given that passing a synchronous handler works, I believe that the typing for the dict value should be adjusted to Callable[[Request, Any], Union[Response, Coroutine[Any, Any, Response]]]

nodes.author: YuriiMotov

Yes, you are right. Typing is incorrect for exception_handlers parameter. It should accept both sync and async handlers.
But, making your exception handler function async should be the first choice (if you don't have heavy computations or other blocking calls).
If you use sync function as exception handler, it will be run using run_in_threadpool and that's less efficient.

I think BaseHTTPMiddleware is bypassing the base exception handlers and your unauthorized_exception_handler method is not getting called correctly. If you really want to make it work with your way of the code structure, here's how it would work:
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi import HTTPException
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware

app = FastAPI()


class UnauthorizedException(HTTPException):
    def __init__(self, detail: str = "未授权的访问"):
        super().__init__(status_code=401, detail=detail)


async def unauthorized_exception_handler(request: Request, exc: UnauthorizedException):
    return JSONResponse(
        status_code=exc.status_code,
        content={"code": exc.status_code, "message": exc.detail},
    )


# 添加异常处理器
app.add_exception_handler(UnauthorizedException, unauthorized_exception_handler)


class auth(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
    def __init__(self, app):
        super().__init__(app)

    async def dispatch(self, request: Request, call_next):
        try:
            raise UnauthorizedException("缺少认证令牌")
        except UnauthorizedException as e:
            return await unauthorized_exception_handler(request, e)


# 添加中间件
app.add_middleware(auth)


@app.get("/protected")
async def protected_route():
    return {"message": "这是一个受保护的路由"}

I have an application which make heavy use of dependencies. I have deeply nested dependencies, since the application has grown. It keeps the code super clean and modular, which is a plus.
I noticed recently that I wasn't able to hit the load performance I needed. I was tinkering with the code trying to figurate out where the bottleneck could be. To my surprise I noticed that the dependencies was the root cause of it. If I completely removed them from my router definition, I'd achieve very high RPS. As soon as I add one, my RPS would drop. With all of them added, I'd get back to where I started. In essence, I go from 1800 -> 200 RPS. These tests where done in my machine, locally, running the the app with fastapi run dev.
I created an MVP to observe this decay. I added a simple main.py with three routes. One without any dependency, a single dependency and a nested dependency. I run the load test on each one of these endpoints individually. I observed very similar behavior.

From left to right, without dependency, single dependency and nested dependency run, respectively. We can clearly see the drop in RPS we can produce. I've tried to keep the tests as objective as possible, by running them back to back in the exact same conditions, but feel free to suggested a better testing method.
I guess my question here is if this is completely expected, since in essence we are calling functions to resolve values at runtime during the request flow? I would expect some degradation of performance, but 10-20% seems extreme.
If the goal of dependencies is not to instantiate clients and keep code modular, as I am doing in my actual app, please educate me :)

I just wanted to say that you should compare endpoints that do equal job. It's useless to compare the performance of endpoint that doesn't accept any parameters with the endpoint that accepts and validates several parameters.
The following code compares 3 endpoints with equal functionality. And it shows that the difference (average) is very small:
from functools import lru_cache
from typing import Annotated, Any

import pydantic_settings
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Request 

app = FastAPI()


class EnvSettings(pydantic_settings.BaseSettings):
    env: str = "LOCAL"


@lru_cache
def _get_env_settings() -> EnvSettings:
    return EnvSettings()


async def get_env_settings() -> EnvSettings:
    return _get_env_settings()


async def common_parameters(
    env: Annotated[EnvSettings, Depends(get_env_settings)],
    q: str | None = None,
    skip: int = 0,
    limit: int = 100,
):
    return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit, "env": env.env}


@app.get("/users-with-nested-dependency/")
async def read_users_with_nested_dependency(
    commons: Annotated[dict[str, Any], Depends(common_parameters)],
):
    return {
        "env": commons["env"],
        "q": commons["q"],
        "skip": commons["skip"],
        "limit": commons["limit"],
    }


@app.get("/users-with-minimal-dependency/")
async def read_users_with_dependency(
    q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100
):
    env = _get_env_settings()
    return {
        "env": env,
        "q": q,
        "skip": skip,
        "limit": limit,
    }


@app.get("/users-without-dependencies/")
async def read_users_without_dependency(request: Request):
    q = request.query_params.get("q")
    skip = int(request.query_params.get("skip", 0))
    limit = int(request.query_params.get("limit", 100))
    env = _get_env_settings()
    return {
        "env": env,
        "q": q,
        "skip": skip,
        "limit": limit,
    }

nodes.author: YuriiMotov
nodes.body:
Usual (non-streaming) response classes expect you pass the content to it.
But sometimes the content could be too big to load it into memory (imagine you need to return the content of 10Gb video file).
In such cases you may want to send response by chunks in order not to hit memory limit.
To do so, you need to create a async generator function that will read one chunk of the file at a time and yield it. Then, attach this generator function to StreamingResponse object and return this object from your endpoint.
FastAPI will call your generator function iteratively and send chunks of the file to client one by one.

Hello @Zhoros,
when you return directly an instance of Response , in your case PlainTextResponse, this is the one that will be used and the one declared in dependecy will be ignored.

nodes.author: YuriiMotov
nodes.body:
You've already answered to your own question)
Do you think it will it be clear if we add the following clarification to docs?
Multiple middleware execution order
When you add multiple middlewares using either @app.middleware() decorator or app.add_middleware() method, each new middleware wraps the application, forming a stack. The last middleware added is the outermost, and the first is the innermost.
On the request path, the outermost middleware runs first.
On the response path, it runs last.
For example:
app.add_middleware(MiddlewareA)
app.add_middleware(MiddlewareB)
This results in the following execution order:


Request: MiddlewareB → MiddlewareA → route


Response: route → MiddlewareA → MiddlewareB


This stacking behavior ensures that middlewares are executed in a predictable and controllable order.

nodes.author: YuriiMotov
nodes.body:
Not sure it's the easiest way, but the following code works:
import asyncio

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from starlette.responses import StreamingResponse

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/stream")
async def stream(request: Request):
    async def event_generator(state: dict[str, int | str]):
        try:
            for i in range(20):  # Simulating a long output from a large model
                state["step"] = i
                await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
                yield f"data: Line {i}\n\n"
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"Error occurred: {e}")
        state["finished"] = True

    state = {"step": 0}  # Shared state object

    async def watch_disconnect(request: Request):
        while True:
            if await request.is_disconnected():
                await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
                is_finished = state.get("finished", False)
                if not is_finished:
                    print(f"Client disconnected at step #{state['step']}")
                break

    asyncio.create_task(watch_disconnect(request))

    return StreamingResponse(event_generator(state), media_type="text/event-stream")


Here, before returning StreamingResponse we run watcher task in the background and pass state objects to it.
We also pass the same state object to generator function.
When client disconnects, StreamingResponse will stop iterating through generator function, but we will have it's last state stored in shared state object.
watch_disconnect function handles client disconnect and reports if client disconnected before finishing sending the response.

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, Query
from fastapi.responses import RedirectResponse
from marimo import create_asgi_app
from pathlib import Path
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Annotated, Literal
from urllib.parse import urlencode


app = FastAPI()


class FilterParams(BaseModel):
    limit: int = Field(100, gt=0, le=100)
    offset: int = Field(0, ge=0)
    order_by: Literal["created_at", "updated_at"] = "created_at"
    tags: list[str] = []


@app.get("/items")
async def marimo_items(
    request: Request, filter_query: Annotated[FilterParams, Query()]
):
    query_params = urlencode(filter_query.model_dump(), doseq=True)
    return RedirectResponse(url=f"/items/?{query_params}")


server = create_asgi_app(include_code=True, quiet=False)
notebooks_dir = Path(__file__).parent.parent / "notebooks"

for filename in notebooks_dir.iterdir():
    if filename.suffix == ".py":
        app_name = filename.stem
        server = server.with_app(path=f"/{app_name}", root=filename)


app.mount("/", server.build())

So, here we have FastApi app with GET endpoint with path /items and marimo app, that has endpoint with another path (/items/).
For FastAPI /items and /items/ are different paths. FastAPI shows nicely-looking docs for /items because that endpoint function was annotated properly.

nodes.body:
Common approach will be to use Redis cache (not sure you need it in this particular case).
But, if you only need to cache this dependency in one worker instance and you don't want to add Redis, you can use cachetools lib:
Install cachetools:
pip install cachetools

Use it:
from time import sleep

from cachetools import TTLCache, cached

cache = TTLCache(maxsize=100, ttl=2)  # TTL = 2 sec

@cached(cache)
def get_token():
    # tokens have a 2 hour lifetime
    import uuid
    LOGGER.warning("new token") # prints every request
    return str(uuid.uuid4())


a = get_token()

b = get_token()

sleep(3)

c = get_token()


assert a == b
assert a != c

nodes.author: YuriiMotov
nodes.body:
I got it!
When the unhandled exception happens in your endpoint, it goes through the whole middleware stack and finally gets to ServerErrorMiddleware. Then ServerErrorMiddleware sends the response. At this moment we are already outside of CORSRiddleware, so, it can't modify the response.
The only way I can see here is to handle exception in the endpoint function, raise custom exception and handle it with exception handlers:
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Request
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
from pydantic import BaseModel

class EdgResponse(BaseModel):
    error_code: int
    error_message: str


class FatalError(HTTPException):
    pass


app = FastAPI()

app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["*"],
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["*"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
)


@app.get("/")
async def index():
    try:
        # do something
        raise Exception("12345")
    except Exception as e:
        raise FatalError(status_code=500, detail=str(e))


def set_exception_handler(app: FastAPI):

    @app.exception_handler(FatalError)
    async def edg_exception_handler(_: Request, exc: FatalError):
        content = EdgResponse(error_code=exc.status_code, error_message=exc.detail)
        return JSONResponse(
            status_code=exc.status_code,
            content=content.model_dump()
        )


set_exception_handler(app)

There is no way to configure FastAPI to run background tasks concurrently, but you can use the following approach:
import asyncio
from fastapi import BackgroundTasks, FastAPI

async def concurrent_tasks(tasks: list[asyncio.Task]) -> None:
    await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

nodes.author: luzzodev
nodes.body:
Hi @jandonov,
When conducting a benchmark to analyze different scenarios and compare various approaches, it’s crucial to ensure the test scenario is well-designed and accurately reflects what you intend to measure.
In your case, there are several issues that likely influenced the results you observed:
1. Isolation
Running all components on the same machine can introduce noise. The sync and async approaches may impose different loads on the system, and those variations can affect performance outcomes. If your goal is to compare the two models purely, this introduces a variable that should be excluded. However, if you're evaluating them within a closed system setup, then including that factor is valid.
2. Context
Concurrency and parallelism are not the same—they're often treated interchangeably but have fundamentally different strengths and limitations, often opposing ones. Understanding which applies to your scenario is essential.
3. Benchmark Accuracy
You must ensure your benchmark aligns correctly with the metrics you intend to measure.
Back to Your Benchmark
What does your test represent?
It appears to simulate a scenario where a maximum of 20 concurrent requests are made, with database response times being nearly negligible (e.g., empty DB, simple queries, local machine).
Are the results expected?
Absolutely. Parallelism doesn’t incur the overhead that concurrency does. Threads are managed in a pool, and with minimal processing time, their efficiency is high. In other words, you're comparing 25 workers handling quick requests in parallel with a single worker processing 25 requests piece by piece.
Here you have another example:
Run 1 Sync -> using time.sleep(0.05)
RT: 53ms
Run 2 Async  -> using asyncio.sleep(0.05)
RT: 73

Whether you're handling 50k or 500k total requests just changes the test's duration, not its structure.
For your specific benchmark only you should expect:
1 Full sync (normal def rouets + synd db operations).
2. Full async (async def routes + async db operations).
3. Mixed (async def rouets + sync db operations).
If the blocking time from the query is less then concurrency overhead or if is so small to be ignored you can switch for sure 2 with 3.
What's Missing in the Test?
You’re overlooking the benefits and role of concurrency.
What happens with 200 users instead of 20 (still with 50k total requests)?
With parallelism, you might cap at 40 available workers, and additional requests will queue or get dropped. In contrast, with async, those extra requests can still be handled concurrently by each worker, allowing better throughput.
What if the endpoint has longer processing times?
The longer the wait, the greater the advantage of async. Async efficiency increases while thread-based parallelism drops off due to idle resource consumption during wait periods.
These are fundamentally concurrency vs. parallelism considerations, not just FastAPI-specific ones.
Another Important Point
Locust simulates load based on users, not requests per second. This is a significant difference. In your case, RPS is a derived metric, not the true throughput. So if the number of users doesn’t exceed your worker limit (e.g., 40), the test always compares direct thread calls vs. the overhead of concurrent execution.
In your case, you're not really measuring the server’s maximum RPS, you're measuring what 20 users can produce.
Conclusions
In general, parallel calls are faster to execute than concurrent ones. However, their major limitation is scalability. You can typically handle far more concurrent requests than parallel ones. The sweet spot is to combine both approaches: use multiple workers, each handling requests concurrently.
Simplified Final Example
Imagine an endpoint calling an AI inference service via HTTP, which takes 5 seconds to respond, and 100 requests arrive simultaneously.
Sync (Thread) Scenario
  t=0   → 100 queued, 0 processed  
  t=5   → 80 queued, 20 processed  
  t=10  → 60 queued, 40 processed  
  t=15  → 40 queued, 60 processed  
  t=20  → 20 queued, 80 processed  
  t=25  → 0 queued, 100 processed  

Async Scenario
  t=0       → 100 queued, 0 processed  
  t≈5 to 10 → 0 queued, 100 processed  

Here, while each sync call may be slightly faster per execution, threads are blocked the entire time, wasting resources.
Even if async takes 5.005 seconds per call (due to overhead), it allows the server to process other requests during that wait, massively increasing throughput.

nodes.author: luzzodev
nodes.body:
Hello @SailorMax,
Few things to cover. This issue actually stems from Starlette’s HTTP middleware: it creates a cached copy of the request by wrapping the ASGI receive function, but it doesn’t handle some cases where the middleware itself consumes the stream (for example, via await request.form()). Once that stream is drained, downstream handlers have nothing left to read.
Starlette discourages and may eventually stop supporting the use of this HTTP middleware, so this form-consumption case is unlikely to be fixed upstream.

if uncomment "print(await request.body())" in authorization() - the problem will gone.

in your authorization() middleware, you force Starlette to read and cache the entire body, so later reads succeed.

if comment "print(await request.form())" in authorization() - the problem will gone.

the middleware never drains the stream, and your endpoint can read it normally.
Also a small sidenotes:
await request.form()
await request.body()
In any case this will raise a  RuntimeError("Stream consumed") so i think this is not exactly a missing case but an explicit decision.

nodes.body:
Your issue is 100% related to CORS handling.
For reference, see the GitHub discussion here: #13717
Middleware Ordering Matters in FastAPI
Since you're building a custom exception handler via middleware, it's important to understand how FastAPI/Starlette middleware works:
Middleware are initialized in declaration order (top to bottom),
But executed in reverse order (bottom to top for incoming requests, and top to bottom for responses).

❌ Your Current Setup
app.add_middleware(CORSMiddleware)
app.add_middleware(GeneralExceptionMiddleware)
Which produces the following flow:
init CORSMiddleware
init GeneralExceptionMiddleware

enter GeneralExceptionMiddleware
enter CORSMiddleware
exit CORSMiddleware
exit GeneralExceptionMiddleware

The problem: if the GeneralExceptionMiddleware returns a response directly (e.g., from a caught exception), the CORSMiddleware never gets to inject the necessary CORS headers, especially on error responses.
✅ Correct Setup
To fix it, reverse the order of your middleware declarations:
app.add_middleware(GeneralExceptionMiddleware)
app.add_middleware(CORSMiddleware)
This leads to the desired flow:
init GeneralExceptionMiddleware
init CORSMiddleware

enter CORSMiddleware
enter GeneralExceptionMiddleware
exit GeneralExceptionMiddleware
exit CORSMiddleware

Now, CORS wraps everything, even error responses, and you’ll get the correct headers like Access-Control-Allow-Origin in all cases.
Declare CORSMiddleware last so it wraps all responses.
This ensures that error responses still include CORS headers.
Remember: declaration order = outermost middleware, but execution is inside-out.

nodes.author: luzzodev
nodes.body:
Hello @liquidcarbon,
About Validation
You're right, this is a known issue. FastAPI preloads default values and injects them during model creation. The same behavior occurs with parameters in Form, Header, and others.
Regarding Your Use of items: str | List[str] = Field()
While the syntax str | List[str] is technically valid in Python 3.10+, it's strongly discouraged to mix types this way for query parameters.
Here’s why:


Multiplicity:
Decide upfront whether the parameter should represent a single value or multiple values.
Supporting both simultaneously leads to ambiguous behavior and parsing inconsistencies.


Format Consistency:
Although there's no hard constraint on how lists should be formatted, it's best to enforce a single, consistent convention.
FastAPI officially supports multiple values using repeated keys: ?foo=bar&foo=baz


This is also OpenAPI-compliant and supported by most HTTP clients and tooling.
Conclusion:
While it is technically possible to achieve what you're asking for, I don't believe it should be better supported or encouraged.
Supporting both single and multiple values in a mixed format leads to ambiguity, complicates validation, and goes against the principles of clear and consistent API design. It's better to choose one approach and design around it for clarity and maintainability.

nodes.body:
FastAPI is currently the most popular asynchronous Python web framework, which is great, and it has a very large community of users.
However, at the moment, we can't help but feel concerned. FastAPI hasn't released a new version for a long time, and the recent updates have mostly been documentation-related (community translations).

nodes.author: DoctorJohn
nodes.body:
Hi, since you're using an UploadFile, FastAPI/Starlette will interpret and store your post data as a multipart form. This is done internally via await request.form() as soon as the request is received. After that, the raw request data is no longer available and therefore can not be accessed via await request.body().
Ironically, if the post data is first accessed via await request.body() it is possible to access it again via await request.form(), because the raw request data can be reinterpreted as multipart form data.
This leaves us with three options:


Option: work with form data in your credential dependency
async def credential(request: Request):
    form = await request.form()


Option: interpret the post data yourself
async def credential(request: Request):
    body = await request.body()  # No longer raises a runtime error


@app.post("/api")
async def read_root(
    request: Request,
    credential: Any = Depends(credential),
):
    form = await request.form()
    file = form.get("file")
    return {"Hello": file.filename if isinstance(file, UploadFile) else "no file"}


Option: start a discussion in the Starlette repo
I'm pretty sure it's a performance optimization that the raw post data is no longer available if it has been accessed via await request.form() first. However, technically, it would be possible to preserve the raw post data in that case.

nodes.author: sachinh35
nodes.body:
Sure, here's my 2 cents on this:

Without going into the specifics of why - all API frameworks, be it in Python, Java or any other programming language treat path parameters as mandatory. This is a contract in the OpenAI spec and that's how the internet works. This is not an issue in Fast API.
There are millions of people who are using OpenAPI for their production loads and I'm fairly certain that a lot of them are using the upsert operation without any issue. So this problem looks very specific to your code otherwise there would have been at least 10s of thousands of issues related to this on the repo.

Getting back to your code - I think your upsert operation is fundamentally wired incorrectly and you always need the user_id as a path parameter. Instead of generating the user_id on the server side, your client should always feed in the user_id. If you want to generate the user_id on behalf of the client, then that's a POST operation altogether as it represents the creation of a new resource rather than an update or insertion of an existing one identified by a path parameter.

nodes.title: response_model_exclude_none=True omitted when response_model=None is set

nodes.author: luzzodev
nodes.body:
Thank you for the update.
Unfortunately, there isn’t a combination of FastAPI settings that will give you exactly the behaviour you’re looking for. This could definitely be documented more clearly and perhaps improved in the future. Here are a few thoughts:
Model validation / serialization on an endpoint:
The response_model parameter (or your return-type annotation, if you omit response_model) is meant to describe the default or “happy-path” response, typically the 200 OK payload. Any attributes you add alongside it (response_model_exclude_none, response_model_include, etc.) are applied to this base response only.
All other response cases, those you would normally raise as HTTPExceptions or return an explicit Response belong in the responses={...} argument. Each entry in responses maps a status code to its own model and description, keeping the OpenAPI schema clean and explicit.
Putting it another way: response_model defines the primary success schema, while responses={...} lists every additional outcome (errors, redirects, edge cases). Mixing those two concepts in a single union often leads to confusing docs and mypy warnings.
The behaviour above is also supported by the fact that FastAPI does not validate a response body against the schema you list under a particular status code. Only the model declared via response_model is runtime-validated. Everything in responses={...} is treated as documentation.
@app.get(
    "/status",
    response_model=StatusModel,           # happy-path schema
    responses={404: {"model": ErrorModel}}
)
async def get_status() -> StatusModel:
    ...
    raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Not found")
For your use case your could write a custom exception handler, return directly the response in the "negative" cases or override the generated openapi schema. Ex: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/additional-responses/#additional-response-with-model

def weak_lru_cache(maxsize=1, typed=False, ttl=None):
    """LRU Cache decorator that keeps a weak reference to self

    Warning: When used in a class, the class should implement __eq__(self, other) and __hash__(self) methods

    Source: https://stackoverflow.com/a/55990799"""

    def wrapper(func):
        @functools.lru_cache(maxsize, typed)
        def _func(_self, *args, ttl_hash=None, **kwargs):
            del ttl_hash  # Unused parameter, but kept for compatibility
            return func(_self(), *args, **kwargs)

        @functools.wraps(func)
        def inner(self, *args, **kwargs):
            return _func(weakref.ref(self), *args, ttl_hash=_get_ttl_hash(ttl), **kwargs)

        return inner

    return wrapper

nodes.author: luzzodev
nodes.body:
Hello @nicolargo,
I cloned your project and debugged the issue so I could give you a more detailed answer.
I suspected from the start that the problem was not caching the computed value, but rather caching the entire response instance.
The issue isn’t limited to the OS you mentioned, it can potentially affect any OS and it stems from a side effect applied to the response headers.
How I tested it
I disabled TTL generation so the cached response would always be returned.
What happens
The Gzip middleware, in addition to compressing the body, also adds or rewrites certain headers such as Content-Length and Content-Encoding.
This operation modifies those headers inside your cached response (a side effect).
On the next request (a cache hit), the headers are not recalculated because that only happens when the response is first created.
The response passes through the Gzip middleware again, but, based on the existing headers, the middleware forwards it directly, assuming it has already been compressed.
At that point an exception is raised because the declared length no longer matches the actual body.
Hope this helps =)

OpenAPI spec doesn't support specifying alternative names for request parameters, so I think this is unlikely to be supported by FastAPI (this will create inconsistency between actual validation and the openapi schema).
For now you can only declare one name for each request parameter (either name or alias).

    my_field: str = Query(alias="myFieldAlias")

Example Code
from enum import StrEnum
from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import FastAPI, Query
from pydantic import BaseModel, BeforeValidator

app = FastAPI()


class Order(StrEnum):
    ASC = "asc"
    DESC = "desc"


class Sorting(BaseModel):
    field: str
    order: Order


def _validate_sorting(raw_sorting: str) -> Sorting:
    field, order = raw_sorting.split(':')

    return Sorting.model_validate(field=field, order=order)


class Pool(BaseModel):
    name: str
    volume: int


@app.get("/pools")
async def get_pools(
    sorting: Annotated[
        Sorting,
        BeforeValidator(func=_validate_sorting, json_schema_input_type=str),
        Query()
    ] = Sorting(field="volume", order=Order.ASC),
) -> list[Pool]:
    pools = [Pool(name="small_pool", volume=10), Pool(name="big_pool", volume=20)]

    return sorted(pools, key=sorting.field, reverse=sorting.order == Order.DESC)
Description
In the FastAPI tutorial, there is a mention of using functional validators—specifically AfterValidator and BeforeValidator. The usage of AfterValidator is straightforward, but the purpose and behavior of BeforeValidator in FastAPI are less clear.
In Pydantic, BeforeValidator can be used to coerce or cast an input type into a different output type. For this purpose, it provides the json_schema_input_type parameter. This could theoretically be leveraged in FastAPI like so:
@app.get("/pools")
async def get_pools(
    sorting: Annotated[
        Sorting,
        BeforeValidator(func=_validate_sorting, json_schema_input_type=str),
        Query(),
    ] = Sorting(field="volume", order=Order.ASC),
) -> list[Pool]:
...
In this case, the idea is to expose the parameter as a string in Swagger (via json_schema_input_type) while internally validating and converting it into a Sorting object. However, this doesn’t seem to work. Instead it shows this:

I understand that similar behavior can be achieved using Depends to handle custom parsing and validation. But if that’s the case, are there any practical use cases for using BeforeValidator directly in FastAPI routes?

nodes.author: YuriiMotov
nodes.body:
Yes, FastAPI is quite straightforward here. If the type of parameter is Pydantic model and it's annotated with Query, it treats every field of that model as separate query parameter.
I think we should consider this as a limitation.
I think something like the code below should work for you:
from enum import StrEnum
from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, BeforeValidator
from pydantic.json_schema import SkipJsonSchema

app = FastAPI()


class Order(StrEnum):
    ASC = "asc"
    DESC = "desc"


class Sorting(BaseModel):
    field: str
    order: Order


class Pool(BaseModel):
    name: str
    volume: int


def _validate_sorting(raw_sorting: str) -> Sorting:
    field, order = raw_sorting.split(":")
    return Sorting(field=field, order=order)


async def get_sorting(
    sorting: Annotated[
        str | SkipJsonSchema[Sorting], BeforeValidator(_validate_sorting)
    ],
) -> Sorting:
    assert isinstance(sorting, Sorting)
    return sorting


@app.get("/pools")
async def get_pools(
    sorting: Annotated[Sorting, Depends(get_sorting)] = Sorting(
        field="volume", order=Order.ASC
    ),
) -> list[Pool]:
    pools = [Pool(name="small_pool", volume=10), Pool(name="big_pool", volume=20)]
    return sorted(
        pools,
        key=lambda x: getattr(x, sorting.field),
        reverse=(sorting.order == Order.DESC),
    )
You can get rid of get_sorting dependency, but you will have to check the type of sorting in your endpoint with isinstance(sorting, Sorting) then

nodes.author: tiangolo
nodes.body:
Thank you for the report @abhi-jha!

Now, with this new dependency getting injected, even on an earlier pinned version which is very surprising, caused our apps to fail deployment. The fastapi-cloud-cli tries to create a /.config file automatically on invocation of fastapi. Given that root path is privileged, caused our app to start failing deployments.

Agreed, this shouldn't happen! Sorry for the inconvenience with it.
We just handled it in fastapilabs/fastapi-cloud-cli#64 and released it. 🤓

Debugging this proved a bit more tedious than it should have.

This sounds very annoying, sorry you had to go through that.

Why make it default opt-in

Agreed with @luzzodev, the idea with standard is to provide a set of curated default standard dependencies that would provide good defaults, the best benefits, developer experience, etc. Including the things that provide high performance, like uvloop and httptools. If there was a better tool used underneath, or a deprecated one that should be removed (e.g. as was the case with ujson and orjson), it should change there as needed. An extra is not an immutable pinned set of dependencies, for that use case, a lock would be better.
The recommended approach to handle dependencies would be to have your main package dependencies in a pyproject.toml or equivalent, and then an additional lock file with the exact set of packages and versions so that the installation can be replicated exactly.
You should probably use uv (https://github.com/astral-sh/uv), they have detailed instructions to use all the best practices in your Dockerfiles: https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/integration/docker/
An alternative would be Poetry, but I suggest uv. If you need requirements.txt then you could use pip-tools.
And as another alternative to all this, if you want to have strict pinned dependencies but still want to only use a single file with everything together, then it's probably better to not include extras for FastAPI (or any other package) and pin each dependency manually. But this would be the equivalent of doing the work of uv by hand, write the lock by hand, in a much more error prone way.
The main point is, by having a lock, you would have very direct visibility into each and all versions, and you would be able to verify in the git diff when one version of any package in all your dependencies is upgraded and if that could affect anything.

from inspect import Signature, Parameter
from inspect import Signature, Parameter
from typing import Annotated, Any

from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends, HTTPException
from fastapi.security import HTTPBasic, HTTPBearer
from starlette.requests import Request

app = FastAPI()


def dynamic_multiple_auth_schemes(*authenticators):
    
    def wrapper(request: Request, **kwargs):
        print(request, kwargs)
        for auth_res in kwargs.values():
            if auth_res is not None:
                return auth_res
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401)
    
    parameters = [
        Parameter("request", Parameter.POSITIONAL_OR_KEYWORD, annotation=Request),
    ]
    for idx, authenticator in enumerate(authenticators, 1):
        name = f"param{idx}"
        parameter = Parameter(
            name,
            Parameter.POSITIONAL_OR_KEYWORD,
            annotation=Annotated[Any, Depends(authenticator)],
        )
        parameters.append(parameter)
    wrapper.__signature__ = Signature(parameters)
    return wrapper

    dependencies=[
        Depends(dynamic_multiple_auth_schemes(HTTPBasic(auto_error=False), HTTPBearer(auto_error=False)))
    ]
)
